rationale: The BOOK ENTRY identifies the 'new name' as 'a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood' — an objective covenant reality that the bearer knows, receives, and keeps. The supplied evidence does not derive that identification. Every printed proof text treats the new name grammatically as an appellation applied to the bearer ('thy name shall be called... Israel,' 'thou shalt be called by a new name,' 'call his servants by another name'), and Genesis 32:28 supplies its own etymology grounding the name in the bearer's changed status ('for as a prince hast thou power with God... and hast prevailed'). Isaiah 62's Hephzibah/Beulah names designate Zion's reversed status (Forsaken to delighted-in, Desolate to married), which supports covenant-marriage imagery but still names the bearer's condition, not a Word or priesthood the bearer keeps. 'Priesthood' and 'Word' appear nowhere in the cited texts, and the supporting chapter explicitly defers the derivation of 'name' to a separate, unsupplied chapter ('the name is a symbol with its own chapter just ahead'). The chapter's covenant sense of 'know' does give a plausible reading of Rev 2:17's secrecy clause, but the common interpretation (God-conferred new identity/status marking covenant belonging) explains that same clause via intimate belonging while also explaining, without strain, the 'called by' constructions and the internal etymologies the book's core cannot accommodate. By the entry's own book-stated method — a symbol is established only when independent witnesses carry the same figure — the triad Word/covenant/priesthood is not established here.
book_core_identification: The 'new name' is not primarily a designation of the bearer's transformed identity but is itself a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood — an objective covenant reality that is known, received, and kept exclusively by the one who bears it.
book_secondary_elaborations: The renewed name includes or constitutes a renewed Word.
The renewed name includes or constitutes a renewed priesthood.
The name is known, received, and kept only by its bearer (exclusivity clause, drawing on Rev 2:17's 'no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it').
unsupported_glossary_assertions: The identification of the new name with a renewed Word — no supplied text or excerpt connects the new name to the Word; the chapter defers this to an unsupplied 'Name' chapter.
The identification of the new name with a renewed priesthood — priesthood is absent from all four printed proof texts and from the supporting chapter.

The claim that the name is something 'kept' — none of the cited texts speaks of keeping a name; 'kept' is imported from the chapter's argument that knowing means commandment-keeping, which the printed references do not themselves state.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's global thesis that knowing, loving, faith, and belief all converge in commandment-keeping is a broader argument not asserted in the entry and is not adjudicated here.
The application of covenant-'knowing' (Amos 3:2; Hos 2:20) to Rev 2:17's 'knoweth' is a chapter-level interpretive move; the entry depends on it but the chapter, not the entry, argues it.

The chapter's sheep/voice/name synthesis from John 10 and its promissory note that 'the name is a symbol with its own chapter just ahead' show the entry's identification rests on material outside the supplied evidence bundle.
The chapter's redefinitions of hate as un-choosing and of works as commandment-shaped deeds are chapter-only claims irrelevant to the glossary ruling.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading: a 'new name' is a God-conferred designation symbolizing the recipient's new identity, character, and status — conversion, covenant belonging, vindication, and (in Revelation) secure, intimate membership in God's people. The name is an appellation marking what the bearer has become before God, not itself a Word, covenant, or priesthood that the bearer keeps.
counter_core_identification: The new name is an appellative token of the bearer's God-given transformed identity and covenant status.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the name is itself a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood; it holds that in every cited text the name is a designation applied to a person or city expressing changed status, which cannot simultaneously be true of a referent defined as an objective Word-covenant-priesthood the bearer receives and keeps.
counter_case: Genesis 32:28 explains the name Israel by the bearer's status and act: 'for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed' — the text's own etymology grounds the name in identity, not in a covenant object.

Isaiah 62:2-4 uses passive appellation grammar ('thou shalt be called by a new name... thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah') and structures the renaming as a status antithesis: Forsaken/Desolate replaced by Delighted-in/Married — a reversal of the bearer's standing.
Isaiah 65:15 opposes the old name left 'for a curse' with 'another name' for God's servants — names functioning as reputational status markers, exactly as the common reading holds.

Revelation 2:17's secret name is naturally read as the overcomer's unique, intimate, God-given identity ('which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it'), a reading that also accommodates ownership and admission-token backgrounds without redefining the name as a Word or priesthood.
The counter unifies all four texts under one consistent function of naming in Scripture — designation of conferred status — with no unsupported steps.
book_explanatory_advantages: The covenant sense of 'know' (Amos 3:2; Jer 22:16; Hos 2:20), argued in the chapter, gives a non-trivial account of why Rev 2:17's name is known only by its receiver: covenant knowledge is relational and exclusive to the party inside the covenant.
Isaiah 62:4-5's marriage imagery (Beulah, bridegroom rejoicing over bride) genuinely ties the renaming scene to covenant renewal, which fits the entry's covenant emphasis.
counter_explanatory_advantages: Explains the uniform 'shall be called' / 'call his servants by' grammar: a name is what one is called, an appellation of the bearer.
Explains Genesis 32:28's internal rationale linking the name to the bearer's prevailing and princely standing.
Explains the Forsaken→Hephzibah and curse-name→another-name antitheses as status reversals of the bearer.
Explains Rev 2:17's secrecy via personal intimacy without needing the unsupplied 'Name' chapter or the unattested priesthood/Word components.
Requires no assertion absent from the texts, whereas the book's triad imports two elements (Word, priesthood) with zero attestation in the printed references.
evidence_book_core_cannot_explain: Genesis 32:28's explicit etymology — 'for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed' — glosses the new name as the bearer's achieved status; a name defined as 'a renewed Word, covenant, and priesthood' cannot account for this internal explanation without abandoning its own identification.

The consistent 'called by' construction (Isa 62:2; 65:15; Gen 32:28): one is called by an appellation, not called by a priesthood or a Word; the book's core has no mechanism for the name functioning as a vocative designation in every cited text.

Isaiah 62:4's paired antithesis (Forsaken→Hephzibah, Desolate→Beulah) makes the new names status-descriptions of the bearer and her land, which the counter explains directly and the book's core can absorb only by adding steps the evidence does not supply.
decisive_sources: Genesis 32:28 (KJV excerpt, with its internal etymology)
Isaiah 62:2-4 (KJV excerpt, appellation grammar and status antithesis)
Isaiah 65:15 (KJV excerpt, curse-name versus another name)
books/symbolic-language/06-knowing-faith-love-and-belief.adoc (covenant sense of 'know'; explicit deferral of 'name' to an unsupplied chapter)
unresolved_objections: The unsupplied 'Name' chapter may contain the derivation of the Word/priesthood components; on this evidence bundle the identification is unestablished, but a future run including that chapter could alter the assessment.

The chapter's covenant reading of 'knoweth' in Rev 2:17 remains a live and interesting possibility that partially motivates the entry's exclusivity clause even though it does not establish the triad identification.
